title: Domain Names - Implementation and Specification

hero.subtitle: The wire format, resource records, and transport details that make DNS work

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1035 specifies the implementation details of the Domain Name System, including the wire format of DNS messages, resource record types, name compression, and transport protocols.

This RFC is the companion to RFC 1034, which describes DNS concepts. RFC 1035 provides the bits-on-the-wire specification that every DNS implementation must follow.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines the exact technical details of DNS: the format of messages on the network, the types of resource records, name compression and the transports. Every DNS implementation must follow it. It is the companion to the concepts in the previous DNS RFC.

sections.title: Message Format
sections.content: All DNS communications use a single message format for both queries and responses:
sections.plainLanguage: DNS uses one message format for both queries and responses. Each message starts with a fixed header that carries flags and counts, followed by sections for the question and for the answers.

sections.title: Resource Records
sections.content:
Resource records (RRs) are the fundamental data elements of DNS. Each RR has a standard format:

NAMEDomain name this record belongs toVariable
TYPERecord type (A, NS, CNAME, MX, etc.)16 bits
CLASSProtocol class (IN = Internet)16 bits
TTLTime to live in seconds32 bits
RDLENGTHLength of the RDATA field16 bits
RDATARecord-type-specific dataVariable

The most important record types defined in this RFC:

AAddress record — maps a name to an IPv4 address
NSName Server — delegates a zone to an authoritative server
CNAMECanonical Name — an alias that points to another name
SOAStart of Authority — zone metadata (serial, refresh, retry)
MXMail Exchange — specifies mail servers for a domain
PTRPointer — reverse DNS lookup (IP to name)
sections.plainLanguage: A resource record (RR) is the basic unit of DNS data. Each has a name, a type (such as A, NS, CNAME, MX or SOA), a class, a time to live in seconds, a length, and type-specific data. For example, an A record maps a name to an IPv4 address.

sections.title: Name Compression
sections.content:
DNS messages use a compression scheme to reduce the size of domain names. Since many names in a message share common suffixes (e.g., .example.com), compression avoids repeating them.

Pointer Mechanism
Instead of repeating a name suffix, a 2-byte pointer indicates an offset within the message where the suffix was previously encoded. The high two bits of the pointer are set to 11, distinguishing it from a label length byte.
Savings
Compression is especially effective in responses with multiple records for the same domain.
Compression Example
Offset 0x0C: 07 example 03 com 00     (full name)
Offset 0x20: 03 www C0 0C              (www + pointer to offset 0x0C)
Offset 0x28: 04 mail C0 0C             (mail + pointer to offset 0x0C)
sections.plainLanguage: DNS shortens messages by not repeating name endings. A two-byte pointer refers back to an earlier place in the same message where that ending, such as .example.com, already appears. Responses with several records for one domain benefit most.

sections.title: Transport
sections.content:
DNS uses both UDP and TCP for transport, each serving different purposes:

Transport
Port
Usage
UDP
53
Standard queries (messages up to 512 bytes, or larger with EDNS0)
TCP
53
Zone transfers (AXFR/IXFR) and responses that exceed UDP size limits

The original 512-byte UDP limit was lifted by EDNS0 (RFC 6891), which allows larger UDP messages (typically up to 4096 bytes). Modern DNS also supports DNS over HTTPS (DoH, RFC 8484) and DNS over TLS (DoT, RFC 7858) for privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS runs over both UDP and TCP on port 53. UDP carries ordinary queries, originally up to 512 bytes. TCP carries zone transfers and responses too large for UDP. Later extensions allow larger UDP messages and encrypted transports.

Damas, J., Graff, M., and P. Vixie, "Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS(0))", RFC 6891, April 2013.

subtitle: The wire format, resource records, and transport details that make DNS work
summary: RFC 1035 specifies how DNS works on the wire. Every query and response uses one message format with a 12-byte header and four sections, resource records carry the data, repeated name suffixes are shortened with two-byte compression pointers, and messages travel over UDP (512 octets or less) or TCP on port 53.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines how DNS messages are built and sent. All queries and responses share one format with a 12-byte header and four sections. Resource records carry the data, repeated name endings are shortened with two-byte pointers, and messages travel over UDP (512 bytes or less) or TCP on port 53.

what is in a dns header

tldr.problem: DNS servers and clients from different vendors need to agree exactly on the bits of a question and an answer.
tldr.mechanism: One message layout serves for queries and responses: a 12-byte header, then question, answer, authority and additional sections made of resource records. Names are labels of at most 63 octets, and repeated suffixes become 2-byte pointers.
tldr.outcome: Any implementation can interoperate, and the 512-octet UDP limit and TCP fallback are defined here.

today: This message format is still what DNS uses. Messages larger than 512 octets are now common through EDNS(0) (RFC 6891), which adds an extra record to advertise bigger UDP sizes. Many record types have been added since, and DNS can also be carried over TLS and HTTPS. Tools such as dig and Wireshark show the header fields described here.

data.title: DNS message layout
data.code:
+---------------------+
|        Header       |  12 bytes
+---------------------+
|       Question      |  the question for the name server
+---------------------+
|        Answer       |  RRs answering the question
+---------------------+
|      Authority      |  RRs pointing toward an authority
+---------------------+
|      Additional     |  RRs holding additional information
+---------------------+

fields.name: ID
fields.desc: Identifier chosen by the program that makes the query. It is copied into the reply so the two can be matched.

fields.name: QR
fields.desc: 0 means the message is a query, 1 means it is a response.

fields.name: Opcode
fields.desc: Kind of query. 0 = standard query, 1 = inverse query, 2 = server status request. Copied into the response.

fields.name: AA
fields.desc: Authoritative Answer. Valid in responses; the responding server is an authority for the name in the question.

fields.name: TC
fields.desc: Truncation. The message was cut short because it was longer than the channel allows.

fields.name: RD
fields.desc: Recursion Desired. Set in a query and copied into the response; asks the server to pursue the query recursively.

fields.name: RA
fields.desc: Recursion Available. Set in a response to say whether the server supports recursive queries.

fields.name: Z
fields.desc: Reserved for future use. Must be zero in all queries and responses.

fields.name: RCODE
fields.desc: Response code. 0 = no error, 1 = format error, 2 = server failure, 3 = name error (name does not exist), 4 = not implemented, 5 = refused.

fields.name: QDCOUNT
fields.desc: Number of entries in the question section.

fields.name: ANCOUNT
fields.desc: Number of resource records in the answer section.

fields.name: NSCOUNT
fields.desc: Number of name server resource records in the authority section.

fields.name: ARCOUNT
fields.desc: Number of resource records in the additional records section.
